section.title: The LORD Directs the Steps
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 16 is bracketed by two of the collection's clearest statements of divine sovereignty over human planning, verse 1 and verse 9, and closes on a third, verse 33, forming a chapter wide meditation on how human effort and God's sovereign hand relate. Between these bookends come sayings on the king's justice, verses 10 to 15, wisdom's worth and humility, verses 16 to 22, and speech and patience, verses 23 to 32.
section.thesis: People plan, speak, and act, but the LORD weighs every motive, determines every step, and governs even the fall of the lot, so that true wisdom commits its works to Him rather than trusting purely in its own planning.
section.frameNote: Four movements: human plans and the LORD's sovereign hand, verses 1 to 9; the king's justice and favor, verses 10 to 15; wisdom's worth, humility, and pleasant words, verses 16 to 22; and speech, patience, and the LORD's sovereignty over the lot, verses 23 to 33.

units.label: Human plans and the LORD's sovereign hand

verses.text: The plans of the {{lev|heart}} belong to man, but the reply of the tongue is from the LORD.
All a man's ways are pure in his own eyes, but his motives are {{takan|weighed}} out by the LORD.
Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved.
The LORD has made everything for His purpose, even the wicked for the day of disaster.
Everyone who is proud in heart is detestable to the LORD; be assured that he will not go unpunished.
By loving devotion and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the LORD one turns aside from evil.
When a man's ways please the LORD, He makes even the man's enemies live at peace with him.
Better a little with righteousness than great gain with injustice.
A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.
A divine verdict is on the lips of a king; his mouth must not betray justice.
Honest scales and balances are from the LORD; all the weights in the bag are His concern.
Wicked behavior is detestable to kings, for a throne is established through righteousness.
Righteous lips are a king's delight, and he who speaks honestly is beloved.
The wrath of a king is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it.
When a king's face brightens, there is life; his favor is like a rain cloud in spring.

units.label: Wisdom's worth, humility, and pleasant words

verses.text: How much better to acquire wisdom than gold! To gain understanding is more desirable than silver.
The highway of the upright leads away from evil; he who guards his way protects his life.
{{gaon|Pride}} goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
It is better to be lowly in spirit among the humble than to divide the spoil with the proud.
Whoever heeds instruction will find success, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD.
The wise in heart are called discerning, and pleasant speech promotes instruction.
Understanding is a fountain of life to its possessor, but the discipline of fools is folly.

units.label: Speech, patience, and the LORD over the lot

verses.text: The heart of the wise man instructs his mouth and adds persuasiveness to his lips.
Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones.
There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death.
A worker's appetite works for him because his hunger drives him onward.
A worthless man digs up evil, and his speech is like a scorching fire.
A perverse man spreads dissension, and a gossip divides close friends.
A violent man entices his neighbor and leads him down a path that is not good.
He who winks his eye devises perversity; he who purses his lips is bent on evil.
Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is attained along the path of righteousness.
He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city.
The {{goral|lot}} is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

lev.gloss: The heart, the seat of planning and intention, verse 1. The chapter's opening line concedes that plans belong to the human heart, while insisting the actual outcome of speech and steps ultimately belongs to the LORD, a tension held together rather than resolved into either bare human autonomy or fatalism.

takan.gloss: To weigh, measure, or examine, used in verse 2 of the LORD weighing human motives. The image assumes that self assessment is unreliable, all a man's ways are pure in his own eyes, while God's evaluation, precise as a scale, sees what self examination alone cannot.

gaon.gloss: Pride or haughtiness, named in verse 18 as what goes before destruction, one of the most quoted lines in the book. Its counterpart, lowliness of spirit, verse 19, is preferred even over sharing plunder with the proud, showing humility valued above gain.

goral.gloss: The lot, a method of decision making by chance used throughout the Old Testament, verse 33. Even here, in what looks like pure randomness, the chapter insists every decision is from the LORD, extending His sovereignty to the smallest, most seemingly arbitrary outcomes.

basic.context: This chapter is framed by two nearly matching statements, people plan their course, but the LORD determines the outcome, verses 1 and 9, and closes with a third variation, even the fall of a lot is decided by Him, verse 33. Between these bookends come sayings on kings, wisdom's worth, humility, and self controlled speech, all resting on the same foundation, human effort matters, but it operates under God's sovereign hand.
basic.hermeneutics: The repeated pairing of human planning and divine determination, verses 1, 9, and 33, is the interpretive key to the whole chapter. It teaches neither passive fatalism, since the chapter still commends diligent planning, verse 3, wise speech, and self control, nor human autonomy, since every outcome ultimately belongs to the LORD. Wisdom here means planning and working faithfully while holding the results with open hands.
basic.originalLanguages: Lev, the heart, verse 1, is where plans originate, though their outcome belongs to the LORD. Takan, to weigh, verse 2, pictures God assessing motives with a precision human self judgment cannot match. Gaon, pride, verse 18, gives one of the book's most famous warnings, and goral, the lot, verse 33, shows God's sovereignty reaching even into what looks like pure chance.
basic.typology: The chapter's confidence that the LORD determines every step, verse 9, and every fall of the lot, verse 33, anticipates the New Testament's fuller revelation of God's sovereign plan worked out even through human wickedness, most climactically in the crucifixion, where the very ones who acted freely and wickedly did 'whatever Your hand and Your plan had predestined to take place,' Acts 4:27 to 28.
basic.christ: This chapter's repeated insistence that human plans finally rest in the LORD's hands reaches its deepest and most redemptive expression in the cross. There, wicked men freely planned and carried out Christ's crucifixion, yet the apostles could say they did only 'whatever Your hand and Your plan had predestined to take place,' Acts 4:27 to 28, the same pattern of human intention and divine determination this chapter describes, but now put to the salvation of the world. Committing one's works to the LORD, verse 3, finds its fullest ground in Christ, who committed Himself perfectly into His Father's hands, even in death, Luke 23:46.
basic.god: God weighs every human motive, verse 2, determines every human step, verse 9, and governs even the fall of a lot, verse 33, showing a sovereignty that reaches into the smallest corners of ordinary life. He is also the standard behind just kingship, verses 10 to 15, and the giver of wisdom more valuable than gold, verse 16.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 4:27-28 describes wicked men doing whatever God's hand and plan had predestined, echoing this chapter's pattern of human intention within divine determination. Ephesians 1:11 speaks of God working all things according to the counsel of His will. James 4:13-15 warns against presuming on one's own plans without regard for the Lord's will. Luke 23:46 has Christ commit His spirit into His Father's hands, embodying verse 3's call to commit one's works to the LORD.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's steady insistence that human planning operates entirely within God's sovereign determination belongs to the Bible's larger story of a God who works all things according to His purposes, even human sin and seeming chance. That story reaches its climax at the cross, where human plans of the worst kind became, in God's hand, the very means of salvation, the pattern of this chapter fulfilled at the deepest possible level.

context.literary:
Proverbs 16 opens a new stretch of the Solomonic collection. Up to this point most sayings set two things against each other with 'but'. From here the sayings more often stand alone or are gathered into clusters, and the LORD takes over the front of the chapter. Eight of the first nine verses name Him or the fear of Him, and the only one that does not, verse 8, is a 'better than' saying that sets righteousness against gain. The result is a deliberate frame: before the book turns to kings, speech and character, it plants the claim that every human arrangement happens under God.

Verses 1 and 9 are close partners. Both set the heart's planning beside the LORD's action, one on speech and the other on steps. In between, verses 2 to 8 work through what the planning looks like when it meets God: motives weighed, works committed, pride refused, devotion and faithfulness that atone, a way that pleases Him, and a small honest income. Verses 10 to 15 then gather the sayings on kings, and the subject moves from one person's plans to public power. The tone is a shift in scale, from a man's heart to a throne.

Verses 16 to 24 return to wisdom, pride and speech, and verses 25 to 30 turn dark with ways that seem right and men who dig up evil, spread strife, entice and wink at mischief. The last three verses of the chapter are a quiet counterweight, with gray hair as a crown, self-control better than conquest, and the lot cast but decided by the LORD. Verse 25 repeats Proverbs 14:12 almost word for word, and verses 2 and 9 echo Proverbs 21:2 and 20:24, so the chapter uses the book's own refrains as pillars.
context.historical:
Kings are all through the middle of this chapter because the sayings were written for a court that served one. Verse 10 says 'a divine verdict is on the lips of a king.' The word translated 'verdict' is the one Deuteronomy 18:10 uses for divination, so in Israel's ears it carried the weight of an oracle, an authoritative decision. In the surrounding nations a king's word was also thought to carry divine sanction. Proverbs borrows the idea and ties it to a condition: the king's mouth must not betray justice. Solomon's famous judgment is the model, 1 Kings 3:28, and Proverbs 20:28 says a king is preserved by loving devotion and faithfulness.

The weights and scales of verse 11 were stones carried in a bag, as Deuteronomy 25:13-16 pictures, and a merchant could keep a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling. The Law called that detestable, and the proverb adds that the true weights come from the LORD, which makes ordinary trade a place of worship. The image of the 'spring rain' in verse 15 is the late rain that ripens the grain, which Deuteronomy 11:14 pairs with the autumn rain. In a land that depended on rainfall, a king's smile was likened to the one thing a farmer could not make.

Verse 33 depends on the practice of casting lots, used in Israel to divide the land, Numbers 26:55, to find a guilty person, Joshua 7:14-18, to choose between the two goats on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:8, and later to settle disputes, as Proverbs 18:18 notes. Lots were not seen as chance but as a way of asking the LORD. The 'gray hair' of verse 31 recalls the command in Leviticus 19:32 to honor the aged.
context.canonical:
The partnership of human planning and divine direction in verses 1, 9 and 33 echoes in many places. Jeremiah says that no one who walks directs his own steps, Jeremiah 10:23, and Proverbs 19:21 and 20:24 repeat the thought. Psalm 33:10-11 sets the plans of the nations against the counsel of the LORD that stands forever. Verse 3's call to commit one's way to the LORD sounds again in Psalm 37:5 and in Peter's 'cast all your anxiety on Him,' 1 Peter 5:7. James takes the proverb as the ground for his warning against saying 'today or tomorrow we will go,' James 4:13-15.

The lot of verse 33 appears in key moments. The sailors cast lots and the lot fell on Jonah, Jonah 1:7. The pur was cast before Haman to pick a day for destroying the Jews, Esther 3:7, and the book of Esther then shows that the LORD had the last word. In Acts 1:24-26 the apostles pray, 'Lord, You know everyone's heart,' and cast lots to choose Matthias, which is the last time lots are used in the New Testament.

Verse 18 on pride is shown in the lives of Uzziah, 2 Chronicles 26:16, and Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel 4:34-37, and taught by Jesus in Luke 14:11 and by James and Peter, who both quote Proverbs 3:34. Verse 25 recalls the Judges refrain, 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes,' Judges 17:6. Verse 32 is taken up in James 1:19-20 and in the call to be slow to anger, which goes back to the LORD's own self description in Exodus 34:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage wanted his hearers to hold two truths together without letting one cancel the other. They are real planners, whose hearts arrange and whose tongues speak, and they are also creatures whose steps are set by the LORD. The chapter does not offer the second truth as a reason to stop planning. Verse 3 says to commit the works, and verses 20 and 22 praise heeding instruction and understanding. It offers it as the reason to plan with open hands and an honest heart.

He also meant to teach the young man who would one day stand before a throne, whether as an official or as a subject. A king's word is serious, a king's anger is dangerous and a wise man can soothe it, verses 10 to 15, yet the king himself answers to the LORD, who owns the scales. So a good official fears God more than he fears the king.

The warnings in verses 25 to 30 were meant to be practical. They describe the men who recruit others toward harm, with winks, whispers and smooth invitations, so the young listener could recognise them. The sage wanted his hearers to find their confidence in verse 20, in the one who trusts the LORD, not in their own ability to read every situation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is description of how God governs and how people tend to fare. The commands are few and clear: commit your works to the LORD, verse 3, acquire wisdom, verse 16, guard your way, verse 17, and control your temper, verse 32. The rest describes, and it should be read as description. Verse 7 says the LORD makes a man's enemies live at peace with him when his ways please Him, but that does not promise that no righteous person will be opposed, as the life of Jesus and the prophets shows. Verse 31 calls gray hair a crown 'attained along the path of righteousness,' and that is a general pattern, since the Bible elsewhere knows of the righteous who die young.

Verse 4 and verse 33 are the places where description most easily turns into a rule. The believer should not take verse 33 as permission to settle ordinary decisions by throwing dice, any more than Acts 1:26 sets a pattern for church governance. It is a statement about who governs outcomes, not a method for finding God's will. In the same way, the idea that the LORD directs every step is a comfort to the trusting and not an excuse for the idle.

debates.question: How do verses 1, 9, and 33 relate human freedom and divine sovereignty?

views.label: Compatibilist, both are fully real and coexist without contradiction
views.case: The chapter never denies that people genuinely plan, work, and even cast lots by their own choice, verse 1's 'plans of the heart belong to man,' while affirming God determines the outcome, holding both truths together exactly as Genesis 50:20 and Acts 4:27-28 do elsewhere in Scripture.

views.label: A a call to humble trust rather than a systematic philosophical claim
views.case: As proverbial wisdom rather than doctrinal treatise, the emphasis of these verses is pastoral and practical, teaching humility and trust in planning, rather than resolving the philosophical mechanics of how divine determination and genuine human choice relate.

debates.bearing: Scripture consistently holds genuine human planning and God's sovereign determination together without treating them as contradictory, and this chapter's repeated refrain functions primarily to humble human self confidence and encourage committing plans to the LORD, rather than to settle every question a philosophical theology might ask of it.

debates.question: What does verse 4 mean by saying God made 'even the wicked for the day of disaster'?

views.label: God ordains some people for destruction from the start
views.case: Read plainly, the line says that the LORD made the wicked with the day of disaster in view. Romans 9:22 speaks of 'vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction,' and Proverbs 16:9 and 33 insist that nothing falls outside His plan. On this view the verse teaches that even the existence and end of the wicked serve His purposes.

views.label: God orders the outcome of wickedness without making anyone wicked
views.case: The verse says the LORD made 'everything' for His purpose and adds that the wicked will meet a day of disaster, that is, that sin has its sentence. It does not say He caused their wickedness. Ezekiel 33:11 says He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and wants them to turn and live, and verse 5 of this same chapter places the guilt on the proud. On this reading the verse is about the certainty of judgment.

debates.bearing: Both views honor the main claim, that no one and nothing falls outside God's rule and that evil cannot escape judgment. The safest reading holds the verse together with Ezekiel 33:11 and Romans 9:22: the LORD is sovereign over the end of the wicked, yet the proverb never blames Him for their choices, and every warning in the chapter calls the reader to turn.

debates.question: How can 'loving devotion and faithfulness' atone for iniquity in verse 6?

views.label: Human kindness and loyalty earn forgiveness
views.case: The verb is the one used for atonement and the line names human virtues. Some readers have taken it to say that acts of mercy cover sin. Daniel 4:27 and similar lines in other books are sometimes offered as parallels.

views.label: God's own covenant love and faithfulness provide the atonement
views.case: The two words are the pair that describe the LORD in Exodus 34:6, 'abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.' On this view the verse looks to God's character as the ground on which sin is covered, and the second line, that the fear of the LORD turns a person from evil, describes the human response.

views.label: Atonement is received, and loyal love is its fruit
views.case: Within the Law, atonement came through the sacrifice God appointed. The proverb then names the evidence in a life: a person marked by loyal love and truth has been forgiven and shows it, as the second line shows the turning from evil.

debates.bearing: The Bible does not teach that human kindness cancels sin, Romans 3:23-26, and the proverb is best read beside Exodus 34:6 and Proverbs 20:28. Forgiveness rests on the faithful love of God shown in the atoning work He provides, and where that love has been received it produces loyalty and truth in the believer.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 speaks of the 'plans of the heart,' and the Hebrew noun is ma'arkhe, from a verb that means to set in order, as troops are arranged for battle or a table is laid. The heart arranges, and the LORD gives the answer. Verse 9 puts the same contrast with two verbs, the heart 'plans,' chashav, and the LORD 'determines,' kun, which means to establish or make firm. The verb comes back in verse 3: 'commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved,' where 'achieved' comes from the same root, so the promise is that the plans will be made firm. The word translated 'commit' is gol, literally to roll. It is the picture of rolling a load from your shoulders onto the LORD, and in Psalm 22:8 the mockers use the same verb of the Righteous Sufferer, who trusts in the LORD.

In verse 10 the 'divine verdict' is qesem, the word Deuteronomy 18:10 lists among the forbidden practices of divination. Here it is used without condemnation, as the weight of a decision that a king speaks on God's behalf. The proverb thereby takes a word from the pagan world and fixes it on a king bound to justice. In verse 11 the 'scales' are pelas, a balance, and 'weights' are literally 'stones,' the stones kept in a bag, which fits Deuteronomy 25:13.

Verse 15 compares the king's favor to a 'rain cloud in spring.' The Hebrew malqosh is the late rain, the rain that makes grain fill, as in Deuteronomy 11:14. The saying is more specific than the English suggests: one season's rain decides the harvest.

In verse 20 the footnote in the BSB notes the possibility 'whoever speaks prudently will find what is good.' The verb, maskil, means to act wisely or to give insight, and the noun that follows, dabar, can mean either 'word' or 'matter,' so the Hebrew line can mean heeding instruction or speaking prudently. Both fit the chapter, which links wise hearing and wise speaking.

Verse 28 calls the slanderer a 'gossip,' nirgan, a whisperer, and the same word is used in Proverbs 18:8 and 26:20, 22. The 'perverse man' of that verse is an ish tahpukhot, a man of twisted things, from a verb that means to turn over. Verse 27's 'worthless man' is ish beliyya'al, and the verb 'digs up' is the ordinary word for digging, used of the pit a person digs in Psalm 7:15, so he excavates evil as one would dig a trap.

Verse 32 describes the one who is 'slow to anger' with the Hebrew 'long of nostrils,' erekh appayim, the phrase the LORD uses of Himself in Exodus 34:6. Anger was seen in the flaring nostril, so a long nose is long breath, a patience that does not burn quickly. The one who 'controls his temper' literally 'rules his spirit,' and the chapter thus ends on the rule of the self.

typology.type: The king whose mouth carries a divine verdict, verses 10 to 15
typology.fulfillment: Israel's kings were meant to speak justice for God and rarely did. Isaiah looks for a king who will delight in the fear of the LORD, who will not judge by what his eyes see or his ears hear, but will judge the poor with righteousness, Isaiah 11:3-4. In Jesus the picture is fulfilled. He says, 'I judge only as I hear. And My judgment is just,' John 5:30, and Revelation 19:11 calls Him Faithful and True, who judges and wages war with righteousness. The type falls short in that earthly kings sometimes spoke justice and sometimes failed it, and could be appeased by a clever courtier. Christ's judgment is never wrong and does not depend on a messenger who pacifies Him.

typology.type: The lot cast into the lap, verse 33
typology.fulfillment: At the cross the soldiers cast lots for Jesus' seamless tunic, John 19:23-24, and John notes that this was to fulfil the Scripture. The soldiers meant only to avoid tearing the cloth, and in the casting of that lot, the most apparently random act in the story, the plan of the LORD was being carried out. It is the proverb at its smallest scale, and the arrangement of the whole crucifixion at its largest, Acts 2:23. The type has limits. Nothing in the proverb makes every lot a sign, and the soldiers' lot is a parable of providence rather than a rule for choosing.

typology.type: Committing one's way to the LORD, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: The verb for 'commit' means to roll one's burden on the LORD. At the cross the bystanders quote Psalm 22:8, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him,' Matthew 27:43, and Jesus' last words are 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46. Here is the proverb lived out at the greatest cost, with a work given wholly to God and a life placed in His hands. The correspondence is the trust, and the difference is the result. Where the proverb promises that plans will be established, Jesus' death is followed by the resurrection, which establishes everything He came to do.

The proverb says that ruling one's temper is greater than capturing a city. Jesus is the one who held back power that no earthly warrior could match. In Gethsemane He tells Peter that He could ask the Father for more than twelve legions of angels, Matthew 26:53, and He does not. In Revelation 5:5-6 the Lion who has triumphed appears as a slain Lamb. His patience also reflects the LORD's own character, 2 Peter 3:9. The type stops short of saying that restraint is only a virtue in a leader: in Christ it is the means by which sinners are saved.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most clearly at the cross, which is where verses 1, 9 and 33 meet. The apostles pray that Herod and Pilate, with the nations and Israel, did what God's hand and will had decided beforehand, Acts 4:27-28, and Peter preaches that Jesus was delivered up by God's set plan, even while 'the hands of the lawless' nailed Him to the cross, Acts 2:23. No one in the story was forced, and every actor chose, yet the outcome was the LORD's. The proverb's pairing of the heart that plans and the LORD who determines is the pattern in which the salvation of the world was accomplished. Peter adds that Christ was known before the foundation of the world, 1 Peter 1:20, so the plan was settled long before the plotting.

It leads to Christ as the perfect committer of his works. Jesus says that He can do nothing by Himself and seeks not His own will but the will of the One who sent Him, John 5:30. In Luke 22:42 He prays, 'not My will, but Yours,' and in Luke 23:46 He commits His spirit into the Father's hands. What verse 3 asks of every wise person is what He did without failing.

It leads to Christ as the wisdom that is better than gold. Verse 16 says getting wisdom is better than gold, and Paul calls Christ 'the wisdom of God,' 1 Corinthians 1:24, with all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Him, Colossians 2:3. The believer who acquires Him has found what verse 16 praised.

It leads to Christ as the King whose face brings life. Verse 15 says that when a king's face brightens there is life. In Christ the face of God shines on sinners, and Paul speaks of the light of the knowledge of God's glory 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. The ancient blessing of Numbers 6:25, that the LORD would make His face shine on His people, is answered there.

It leads to Christ in the matter of pride. Verse 18 says pride goes before a fall, and the pattern of the gospel is the reverse: He who was in the form of God humbled Himself and was exalted, Philippians 2:8-9.

The caution is that the chapter's sayings on kings are not all predictions of the Messiah. They describe the standard a king should meet, and Christ is the King who meets it perfectly.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter says about God is that He governs the ordinary. Not just the great events, but the plans of the heart and the reply of the tongue, verse 1, the steps of the traveller, verse 9, the honest weights in the merchant's bag, verse 11, and even the lot, verse 33. There is no corner of life where He is absent. Job 42:2 says no plan of His can be thwarted, and Isaiah 46:10 has Him say that His purpose will stand.

He is also the one who weighs motives. Verse 2 says that all a man's ways are pure in his own eyes, which is the universal human condition, and the LORD weighs the spirit. Proverbs 21:2 repeats it and Jeremiah 17:10 gives the divine voice, 'I, the LORD, search the heart.' The One who governs also judges, and neither is allowed to swallow the other.

He is holy and opposes the proud. Verse 5 says the proud are detestable and will not go unpunished, and Proverbs 8:13 has wisdom say, 'I hate arrogant pride.' His opposition to pride is the other side of His grace to the humble, verse 19.

He is merciful. Verse 6 says that iniquity is atoned for, which means that the God who weighs hearts also provides a covering. His loving devotion and faithfulness, Exodus 34:6, are the ground. And verse 7 gives His quiet care: when a man's ways please Him, He can make even his enemies live at peace with him.

There is a tension the chapter does not hide. God made 'even the wicked for the day of disaster,' verse 4, and yet He holds the proud responsible, verse 5, and gives commands that assume a real response. The Bible never reconciles these in a formula. It asks us to trust a God who is both sovereign and just, and it points to the cross as the place where both are fully displayed.

He is also the God of justice in public life. The true scales are His, verse 11, and a throne is established by righteousness, verse 12. Courts and markets are His business.

For worship, the chapter calls for the humility of a person who knows his steps are set by another. The right response is trust, which Proverbs 3:5-6 calls leaning not on our own understanding, and rest, since the One who directs the steps is the One who can be trusted with the outcome.

crossReferences.note: The prophet confesses that a man's way is not his own and that no one who walks directs his own steps. It is verse 9 in the form of a confession. Jeremiah says it in a time of crisis, which shows that the doctrine of God's direction is a comfort for the troubled, not only a point of theory.

The king's heart is a waterway in the LORD's hand, and He turns it where He pleases. It joins verses 1 and 9 with the royal sayings of verses 10 to 15, so that even the greatest power in the land is steered by Him, as a farmer steers a channel of water.

James scolds people who plan a year of business with no thought of the Lord's will, and tells them to say, 'If the Lord is willing.' It turns the proverb into a habit of speech. The plan is allowed, but it has to be offered to God.

The believers pray that Herod, Pilate, the nations and Israel did only what God's hand and will had decided beforehand. It is the clearest New Testament example of verse 9: human choices, real guilt and a divine plan all in one event, with salvation as the result.

Haman casts the pur, the lot, to choose the day on which the Jews will be destroyed. The story then reverses the day. It reads as a narrative commentary on verse 33: the lot falls where it falls, and the LORD decides what it means.

After praying, 'Lord, You know everyone's heart,' the apostles cast lots to choose Matthias. It shows verse 33 acted on by believers who asked the LORD for the decision. It is the last use of lots recorded in the New Testament, since the Spirit comes in the next chapter.

Nebuchadnezzar, a king who boasted of his own power, loses his sanity and recovers it when he raises his eyes to heaven. He then praises the One whose dominion is everlasting. His story is verse 18 told as a biography, with the fall coming after the pride and honor after the humbling.

The psalmist says, 'Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it.' It is the language of verse 3 in a prayer, and it supplies the object of the promise: it is the LORD who acts, not the one who commits.

The Law forbids two differing weights in the bag and calls dishonest dealing detestable to the LORD. Verse 11 is built on this, and turns the prohibition into a statement about the source: honest scales are His, so cheating in trade is a wrong against Him.

The saying is repeated almost word for word in verse 25: there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death. The repetition marks it as one of the book's pillars. Verse 2's pure-in-his-own-eyes motive is the same blindness seen from the inside.

Paul says God works all things together for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose. It is the New Testament shape of verses 4 and 9, with the added assurance that His rule is directed toward the good of His people.

Christ humbled Himself and became obedient to death, and God exalted Him to the highest place. This is the inverse of verse 18 at its best: the one who goes down willingly is raised up, and the pattern that destroys the proud is the path by which He is glorified.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with human beings who chose what looked good and pleasing to the eye and what seemed right, Genesis 3:6, and Proverbs 16:25 describes the road that followed, a way that seems right to a man but ends in death. Babel is the same story at the scale of a city. The builders say 'let us make a name for ourselves,' and the LORD comes down and scatters them, Genesis 11:4-8. Human planning, left to itself, always overreaches.

Against that backdrop the Bible keeps showing a God who works through human plans, even bad ones. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant it for good, Genesis 50:20. The nations plot and the LORD frustrates their plans, Psalm 33:10-11. The pur is cast, and the people of God are not destroyed. Kings rise and fall, and the proverbs about their justice, their anger and their favor are tested by their histories, which mostly show how far they fall short of verse 10.

The story reaches its center at the cross, where the sinful plans of Herod, Pilate and the crowd were exactly what God's hand and will had decided beforehand, Acts 4:27-28. After that, the lots are no longer cast to find God's will. The apostles use them once in Acts 1:26 and then the Spirit leads.

The story finishes in a world where the rule of God is plain. The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, Revelation 11:15, and the rider on the white horse is called Faithful and True, and judges with righteousness, Revelation 19:11. The One on the throne says, 'Behold, I make all things new,' Revelation 21:5. The proud are gone, the scales are true and the wise who committed their ways to the LORD discover that their plans were established. The doctrine of Proverbs 16 stops being a thing to be believed and becomes the plain fact of the new creation.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between human planning and divine sovereignty in verses 1 and 9?

options.text: People genuinely plan their course, but the LORD ultimately determines the outcome and the steps.
options.note: Both verses state exactly this, affirming real human planning within God's sovereign determination.

options.text: Human planning is entirely meaningless and has no real role.
options.note: The verses affirm genuine human planning, not its meaninglessness.

options.text: God has no involvement in the outcome of human plans.
options.note: This directly contradicts the verses, which explicitly credit the LORD with determining the outcome.

options.text: Only kings' plans are subject to God's determination.
options.note: The verses speak generally of 'a man,' not a category restricted to kings.

quiz.q: According to verse 2, why does a person need God's evaluation of their motives?

options.text: Because all a man's ways seem pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs motives with true accuracy.
options.note: This is the exact reasoning of the verse, exposing the unreliability of self assessment.

options.text: Because human motives are always obviously wicked to everyone, including oneself.
options.note: The verse's point is nearly the opposite, self perception is deceptively favorable, not obviously wicked.

options.text: Because God is uninterested in motives, only actions.
options.note: The verse specifically names motives, not merely outward actions, as what God weighs.

options.text: Because only religious leaders need this kind of evaluation.
options.note: The verse speaks generally of any person's ways and motives, not a specialized class of leaders.

quiz.q: What does verse 18 warn, and how is it usually summarized?

options.text: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
options.note: This is the exact and famous wording of the verse.

options.text: Pride always leads directly to great success.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's actual warning.

options.text: Only kings need to worry about pride.
options.note: The warning is general, applicable to anyone, not restricted to kings.

options.text: Humility is a sign of weakness to be avoided.
options.note: The surrounding verse, 19, actually commends lowliness of spirit as preferable to pride, the opposite of this option.

quiz.q: What does verse 33 say about the casting of lots?

options.text: Even though the lot is cast into the lap, its every decision comes from the LORD.
options.note: This extends divine sovereignty even to what looks like pure chance.

options.text: The casting of lots operates entirely outside of God's control.
options.note: The verse claims the opposite, every decision from the lot is from the LORD.

options.text: Casting lots was forbidden in ancient Israel.
options.note: Casting lots was a recognized and legitimate practice in the Old Testament, not forbidden.

options.text: It applies only to legal disputes in a courtroom.
options.note: The proverb's principle is stated generally about the lot, not restricted to legal contexts alone.

quiz.q: How does this chapter's teaching on divine sovereignty over human plans connect to Christ?

options.text: At the cross, wicked human plans became, under God's sovereign hand, the very means of salvation, as Acts 4:27-28 describes.
options.note: This directly applies the chapter's pattern of human intention within divine determination to the crucifixion.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament's account of the cross.
options.note: Acts 4:27-28 explicitly uses this same pattern to describe the crucifixion.

options.text: It teaches that Christ's death was purely accidental and unplanned by God.
options.note: Acts 4:27-28 explicitly says the crucifixion happened according to God's plan, not by accident.

options.text: It shows that human choices played no real role in the crucifixion.
options.note: Acts 4:27-28 affirms both real human intention and divine predetermination together, not the elimination of human choice.

questions: Verse 3 says to commit your works to the LORD. What plan or project are you currently holding so tightly that you have not truly entrusted its outcome to God?
Verse 2 warns that our own ways always seem pure to us. Where might you need someone else's honest perspective because your own self assessment could be off?
Verse 18 warns that pride goes before a fall. Is there an area of confidence in your life that has quietly slipped into pride rather than humble trust?
Verse 24 says pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet and healing. Who could use a genuinely kind and encouraging word from you today?
Verse 32 says one who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city. Where do you most need self control this week, and how might you invite God's help there specifically?

translationNotes.note: This verse can also be rendered 'whoever speaks prudently will find what is good,' a variant reading that shifts the emphasis slightly from heeding instruction to prudent speech.
The phrase describing the worthless man's speech can also be rendered 'and what is on his lips,' a minor variation describing the same destructive, fire like speech.
